challenges.situation: Your company is one of 15 firms bidding on a government infrastructure contract. You estimate the project will cost $8M to execute. You want to win. What does the winner's curse tell you about how to bid?

options.text: Bid above $8M (include profit margin) but NOT aggressively below — because with 15 bidders, whoever estimates lowest probably underestimated costs, and winning means you're likely the one who got the math wrong
options.feedback: The winner's curse in procurement: with 15 bidders, the 'winner' (lowest bidder in a contract auction) is the one who underestimated costs the most. Bidding at break-even or below maximizes winning probability but guarantees losses when reality exceeds your estimate. You should bid ABOVE your estimate (option D is close but 'unknown risks' isn't the same as 'winner's curse adjustment'). The correct framing: discount your optimism about costs, don't amplify it.

options.text: Bid at exactly $8M (break-even) to maximize your chance of winning
options.feedback: Not quite. The winner's curse in procurement: with 15 bidders, the 'winner' (lowest bidder in a contract auction) is the one who underestimated costs the most. Bidding at break-even or below maximizes winning probability but guarantees losses when reality exceeds your estimate.

options.text: Bid well below $8M to ensure you beat all 14 competitors
options.feedback: Not quite. The winner's curse in procurement: with 15 bidders, the 'winner' (lowest bidder in a contract auction) is the one who underestimated costs the most. Bidding at break-even or below maximizes winning probability but guarantees losses when reality exceeds your estimate.

options.text: Bid 20% above your estimate to account for unknown risks
options.feedback: Not quite. The winner's curse in procurement: with 15 bidders, the 'winner' (lowest bidder in a contract auction) is the one who underestimated costs the most. Bidding at break-even or below maximizes winning probability but guarantees losses when reality exceeds your estimate.

challenges.situation: At a charity auction, a person who planned to spend $100 ends up paying $500 for a bottle of wine worth $40. The room was electric with bidding energy.
challenges.question: What force overrode their pre-set budget?

options.text: Scarcity — competitive arousal triggered by visible rivals + incremental 'just $10 more' framing + social proof that others want it = emotional override of rational budget
options.feedback: While status (B), charity motivation (C), and competitive identity (D) may contribute, the core mechanism is scarcity-driven competitive arousal: rivals bidding creates urgency (scarcity of the item + scarcity of 'winning opportunity'), each increment feels small ('just $10 more'), and others' bids validate value (social proof). The auction STRUCTURE exploits these biases — not the individual's character flaws.

options.text: Status — they wanted to appear generous in front of the crowd
options.feedback: Not quite. While status (B), charity motivation (C), and competitive identity (D) may contribute, the core mechanism is scarcity-driven competitive arousal: rivals bidding creates urgency (scarcity of the item + scarcity of 'winning opportunity'), each increment feels small ('just $10 more'), and others' bids validate value (social proof). The auction STRUCTURE exploits these biases — not the individual's character flaws.

challenges.back: In competitive bidding for uncertain-value items, the winner is the person who overestimated the most. Winning IS evidence of overpaying.

challenges.instruction: Match each concept to its description:

pairs.right: Maximizes competitive escalation and winner's curse — great for sellers, bad for buyers
Incentivizes honest bidding since you pay second price — reduces overpayment

pairs.left: Ken Binmore's 3G spectrum design (5 licenses, 4 incumbents)
pairs.right: Guaranteed new-entrant competition — prevented collusion among existing players

pairs.left: 'Just $50 more' thinking across 10 rounds of bidding
pairs.right: Incremental framing that disguises total overpayment — anchor to total, not increment

pairs.left: Setting your maximum before entering the auction room
pairs.right: Pre-commitment device against in-the-moment competitive arousal override

challenges.context: Which response shows better understanding of the underlying dynamics?

scenarioA.label: Playing to win
scenarioA.text: I know what this is worth and I'm going to win it. If others are bidding this high, it validates my estimate. Just one more bid and I'll have it.

scenarioB.label: Playing to not lose
scenarioB.text: I set my maximum before entering. If winning requires exceeding it, I stop — because winning an auction is statistical evidence I'm the biggest overestimator in the room. I ask who designed these rules, and in whose interest.

challenges.explanation: The second response shows structural awareness — recognizing the game and changing it, rather than just playing harder within the existing frame.

principle.text: The winner's curse: in any competitive bidding for an uncertain-value asset, the winner is systematically the person who overestimated the most. Winning is evidence of overpaying.
principle.subtext: Auction design determines behavior: the same rational bidders produce wildly different outcomes under different rules. English (ascending) auctions maximize competition and extraction. Sealed second-price (Vickrey) auctions produce honest bidding. The game's rules shape the game's outcome.

reflection: Where are you in a competitive bidding situation right now? Is winning actually evidence that you overvalued what you're fighting for?
